Innovation and influence are very distinct phenomena. Bob Dylan, for instance, didn’t invent folk
music: He borrowed extensively from Woody Guthrie, Pete Seeger and others in the folk revival
movement of the fifties and sixties, yet he became far more influential than any of them. Such is
the relationship between Warren Buffett and earlier finance and investing writers, especially
Benjamin Graham, author of The Intelligent Investor. Buffett didn’t dream up most of the ideas
that he espoused — many came straight out of Graham’s teachings — but he brought them to the
masses through the Berkshire Hathaway Inc. annual letters and gave us all a proof of concept
through the company’s extraordinary performance. In doing so, he earned his place as our greatest
investor and our leading finance and investing writer. Without Buffett, we may not be talking about
Graham at all today. So, it was with a tinge of sadness that I learned last week that Buffett was
poised to relinquish his most important annual writing exercise: the Berkshire letter. It is the end
of an era, and a time to reflect on Buffett’s accomplishments.

Over the years, Buffett’s most memorable theme was the flightiness of ‘Mr. Market’ and the need
to stay focused on intrinsic value. For Buffett, Mr. Market — a character first conceived by
Graham — was forever doomed to live with “incurable emotional problems,” as he wrote in
Berkshire’s 1987 letter4. At times Mr. Market was euphoric (prices were too high), and at others
he was deeply depressed (prices were too low), but investors always had the discretion to ignore
him or take him up on his occasionally bargain-bin prices.

The key, for Buffett, was to make sure you did your homework and had a firm grasp on the intrinsic
value of your would-be investments. “Indeed, if you aren’t certain that you understand and can
value your business far better than Mr. Market, you don’t belong in the game,” Buffett wrote. And
indeed, Buffett went on to prove that he belonged in the game, avoiding dot-com bubble stocks in
the late 1990s, building a very conservative portfolio ahead of the financial crisis, and then
pouncing when the crashes created opportunities.
SOURCE:https://www.bloomberg.com/opinion/articles/2025-11-04/buffett-s-annual-letters-a-

The water was clear and bright. After days in the shade, sunlight now cut through the rough surface,
sending shimmering rays dancing across the rocky bed of the river, and illuminating the patches
of bright green algae that carpeted the rocks of deeper, slower pools. The fish gained speed, then
hurled herself above the water line, over the rocks that created a minor fall in the river. Above the
water line, the fish did not notice that the land here held only a remnant of the forest. The riverbank
was open, aside from a still-developing layer of shrubbery and the few remaining blackened
skeletal trees that dotted the riverside. The fish didn’t notice any of this, of course. She had no
awareness of the fire-scarred land or new life that was steadily reclaiming once bare soil. She
pushed ahead, moving steadily against the current. The sunlight illuminated the squirming bodies
of larvae caught in the current. The fish felt, somewhere in the recesses of her mind, the almost-
stirring of an extinguished drive-the urge to swallow them.

That urge remained a whisper in her mind. It did not surface in her body, but she felt its absence
as she swam past the would-be feast. She had once been a fish that ate larvae. Now, she was not.
Simple. She had, not so long ago, lived in the deep sea. Her lithe silver body pulled saltwater
through her gills as she explored the dark depths, feeding on its bounty. Now, she fought her way
upstream in the clear, saltless water. She remembered this taste- this fresh stream water and the
heaviness of her body in its currents. She was getting close. She did not know how she knew this
and did not wonder. But she was getting close.

She would soon make it back to the place her life had begun. There was nothing else for her. This
was right; it was where she belonged. The fish was aware that this pull was a reversal of polarity-
the same sort of tug had once compelled her down this stream and out to the sea. She had once
abandoned these shallow fresh waters for the salty depths. At the time, the need to find the sea had
felt all-consuming, and she believed she would never return to these waters. She had once raced
down these eddies with the same fervor that now compelled her to throw herself up them. She had
needed to leave. And now, she needed to return.

Sadly, the Srikakulam crowd collapse at a private, unregistered temple on a day when high footfall
was expected is hardly surprising. Reports indicate one combined entry and exit, public use of an
under-construction area, inadequate stewardship, severe capacity overshoot, and weak
infrastructure. The Hathras crowd crush in 2024 followed an event in which permission was
reportedly granted for only a third of the crowd that attended, and investigations cited inadequate
exits and gaps in planning and supervision. The 2011 Sabarimala crush also revealed systemic
weaknesses in circulation control on a day with predictable surges and a trigger that became lethal
due to constrained pathways. These incidents had different proximate triggers but the same causes
of failure: reciprocal pedestrian flows and shared gates, weak physical public infrastructure, and a
lack of real-time density monitoring. India already has guidance to anticipate these failures,
including the 2014 National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) guidelines and the National
Building Code (NBC). Indian authorities have already demonstrated a feasible path from guidance
to operations, including in recent Sabarimala seasons and with the Integrated Command and
Control Centre operating at Tirumala. This includes licensed plans compliant with NDMA or NBC
prescriptions; calculated occupancy; certified structures that prevent bidirectional flows; real-time
density control by trained stewards; and real-time communications and crowd analytics. The
persistence of stampedes stems from the gap between guidance and enforced practice.

That almost 80% of stampedes in India occur at religious gatherings or pilgrimages is not
coincidental. Pilgrim and congregational events often proceed without any licence that ties
permission to a crowd safety plan that can be tested for compliance. Authorities often infer the
capacity from the space available, rather than what can be estimated from egress options and
evacuation times, tolerate bad or no gating plans, accept temporary barricades without certified
load ratings, and do not cordon off areas with construction materials. Public safety is a process and
its absence, including during crowding disasters, is rarely due to single-point failures. The
Srikakulam incident aligns with a known risk pattern and only disciplined adoption of the
country’s own codes, enforced by licensing, will reverse it. India also needs a policy culture that
treats religious events as engineered systems requiring licensing and auditing.


SOURCE:https://www.thehindu.com/opinion/editorial/depressing-pattern-on-the-srikakulam-

Over the last three decades, there has been a consistent criticism of governments and private actors
who make environmental policy: Those who seek to protect “nature” know very little about living
in and with it. Arguably, aside from their good intentions, they are accused of drawing a false
disjunction between humans and the environment, including other animals. A research paper
published in Ambio surveyed 56,968 people across 61 countries to assess their level of “nature-
connectedness”. A psychological concept, nature-connectedness seeks to measure the relationship
— or lack thereof — between people and flora and fauna. Several studies have demonstrated that
such connections impact well-being and are correlated with how people act towards the
environment.

According to the study, Nepal is the most nature-connected, followed by Iran, South Africa, and
Bangladesh. India, in 22nd place, is at the upper end of the middle, while the UK, Spain, Japan,
Germany and Canada bring up the rear. Clearly, political activism is not a factor in how close
people are to nature. Germany, Canada and the UK, for example, have far stronger Green parties

than Iran. But people there are, going by the study, less likely to form bonds outside of homo
sapiens. “Spirituality” correlates positively with connectedness, whereas ranking highly on the
World Bank’s Ease of Doing Business index is the opposite.

Does the study, then, insinuate at a return to the old binary between the economy and the
environment, between “development” and “growth”? Hopefully not. The better lesson to draw
from it might be to listen, learn and find a balance. The people surveyed in the countries at the top
of the list also want “development.” The answer might well be to talk to those who live with nature,
and listen to their views before planning to make cities and countries more “green” and “smart”.

a-lesson-on-development-vs-environment-10344409/

The IPO (initial public offering) market in India continues to see a flurry of activity. Firms across
a range of sectors, from LG Electronics to Tata Capital, are increasingly tapping the primary
markets. And it’s not just the larger firms. In recent years, smaller and mid-sized companies, and
even start-ups, like eyewear firm Lenskart, stockbroker Groww and fintech firm Pine Labs, are
flocking to the markets. There are expectations for public offerings this year that surpass those of
last year. Globally, India, along with the US and China, accounted for the bulk of IPO activity
during the third quarter of the year as per EY. All this indicates the Indian markets' capacity to
absorb large issues.

There is a strong appetite from both institutional and retail investors; the latter are seeing
participation beyond the Tier 1 cities. The sharp increase in the number of demat accounts over
the past few years and the continuing surge in SIP flows are indicative of the growing share of

household savings flowing into the markets. The stock market regulator had also recently made
changes to the IPO framework to increase institutional investor participation. But this surge in
liquidity sits uncomfortably with concerns over stretched market valuations. Questions have been
raised about the steep valuations being sought by some companies. In recent months, some IPOs
have underperformed due to aggressive pricing — shares of many companies are trading around
or below their offer price, according to some analysts. But, even IPO investors have invested for
listing-day gains — as per an earlier SEBI study, individual investors sold 50 per cent of their
shares within a week of their listing.

The public offerings can be used for various purposes — for financing firms’ expansion plans or
by existing investors, such as venture capital or private equity firms to exit. Of the Rs 1.17 lakh
crore raised this year, around a third represents investor or promoter exits as per a Kotak study.
This suggests that promoters and early investors, who hold significant stakes, are using this
opportunity to cash out, with the returns generated being either repatriated or deployed across asset
classes. Recent reports indicate that the IPO pipeline remains healthy. The sentiment among retail
investors also seems to be strong, even as the steep valuations, in some cases, are hard to ignore.

The completion of one year since the 2025 Pahalgam attack has brought renewed focus on India–
Pakistan relations, particularly in the context of cross-border terrorism and regional security. The
attack, which targeted civilians in Jammu and Kashmir, had led to heightened tensions between
the two countries and intensified diplomatic exchanges. Over the past year, India has maintained
a firm position on issues related to terrorism, emphasising the need for accountability and stronger
counter-terror mechanisms.

The anniversary has also been marked by increased security measures in sensitive regions, along
with continued monitoring of cross-border activities. Diplomatic relations between the two
countries remain limited, with engagements largely confined to multilateral platforms. The broader
context includes ongoing concerns related to ceasefire agreements, infiltration attempts, and
regional stability in South Asia.

The developments surrounding the anniversary highlight the persistent challenges in bilateral
relations, where security concerns continue to dominate the agenda. The situation also reflects the
complex interplay between diplomacy, defence preparedness, and international pressure in
managing relations between the two nuclear-armed neighbours.

In 2026, Odisha became the first Indian state to implement a Marine Spatial Plan (MSP), marking
a significant step in coastal and marine governance. The initiative aims to regulate the use of ocean
resources by allocating specific zones for activities such as fishing, tourism, conservation, and
shipping. The plan has been developed with technical support from international organisations and
is aligned with India’s broader commitments to sustainable ocean management.

Marine Spatial Planning is a globally recognised approach used to balance ecological protection
with economic activities in marine areas. Odisha’s coastline, which stretches along the Bay of
Bengal, is ecologically sensitive and economically significant, supporting fisheries, ports, and
biodiversity hotspots. The MSP is expected to improve coordination between different
stakeholders and reduce conflicts over resource use.

The development also reflects India’s increasing focus on the blue economy, which emphasises
sustainable use of ocean resources for growth, employment, and environmental protection.
Odisha’s initiative is being seen as a pilot model that could be replicated in other coastal states in
the future.

 The evolution of international air law from the Paris Convention of 1919 to the Chicago
 Convention of 1944 represents a fundamental shift in the regulation of global aviation,
 transitioning from a primarily European-centric framework to a truly international system designed

CLAT 2027 Mock Test – 18                                                12 Minutes to CLAT

 to accommodate the explosive growth of air travel following World War II. The Paris Convention,
 officially the Convention Relating to the Regulation of Aerial Navigation, was the first
 comprehensive international agreement to codify the principle of state sovereignty over airspace,
 declaring that every state had complete and exclusive sovereignty over the airspace above its
 territory.

 This foundational concept, enshrined in its Article 1, directly countered earlier proposals that
 airspace should be considered free and open, much like the high seas. The Paris Convention
 established the International Commission for Air Navigation, which was tasked with collecting
 data and proposing amendments to technical annexes concerning matters like aircraft registration,
 airworthiness, and navigation maps. However, the Paris framework was limited in its global reach,
 as it was largely a product of European powers and did not secure universal participation.
 Moreover, it drew a clear distinction between civil aircraft and state aircraft, such as military and
 customs aircraft, with the latter category being excluded from the right of innocent passage and
 requiring special authorization to overfly or land in foreign territories.

 This principle of nationality, wherein an aircraft possessed the legal character of the state in which
 it was registered, was firmly established and required that registration be made in a public register
 accessible to other states. The onset of World War II, however, demonstrated both the inadequacies
 of the Paris regime and the immense strategic importance of air power, prompting Allied nations
 to begin planning for a new post-war order even as hostilities continued. This planning culminated
 in the Chicago Convention of 1944, which fundamentally restructured international air law by
 creating the International Civil Aviation Organization as a permanent specialized agency of the
 United Nations to oversee cooperation and standard setting.

 The Chicago Convention reaffirmed the core principle of absolute sovereignty from Paris, but
 expanded its scope by explicitly addressing both scheduled and non-scheduled air services,
 establishing the five freedoms of the air through separate agreements, and mandating that all
 charges for airports and air navigation facilities be published and communicated to ICAO. It also
 refined the classification of aircraft, ensuring that the nationality principle applied uniformly to all
 aircraft engaged in international navigation, while continuing to exempt state aircraft from
 automatic overflight rights. The Chicago regime thus created a durable legal architecture balancing
 national sovereignty with the practical necessities of international air commerce.

 The functional phase of a treaty, following its entry into force, is governed by established rules
 regarding its observance, application, and interpretation. These principles, primarily codified in
 the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (VCLT), ensure stability in international relations.
 The cornerstone is pacta sunt servanda (Article 26), which mandates that every treaty in force is
 binding upon the parties and must be performed by them in good faith. Reinforcing this, Article

CLAT 2027 Mock Test – 18                                                12 Minutes to CLAT

 27 prevents a state from invoking its internal law, including its constitution, as a justification for
 treaty non-compliance.

 The application of treaties is subject to specific parameters. Under Article 28, treaties are not
 retroactive, meaning they do not bind a party regarding acts or facts that occurred before the treaty's
 entry into force for that state. Article 29 establishes that a treaty binds each party in respect of its
 entire territory, unless a contrary intention is expressed. Where states conclude successive treaties
 on the same subject, Article 30 provides the framework for determining which instrument prevails.

 The interpretation of treaties is governed by a general rule articulated in Articles 31-33. The
 primary approach is textual: a treaty must be interpreted in good faith according to the ordinary
 meaning of its terms in their context, and in light of its object and purpose. The context includes
 the preamble and annexes. Crucially, subsequent agreements between the parties on interpretation,
 and their subsequent practice in applying the treaty, are to be taken into account. Supplementary
 means, such as the negotiating history (travaux préparatoires), may only be consulted to confirm
 the meaning derived from this general rule, or when the primary interpretation leaves the meaning
 ambiguous.

 Separate from questions of application are grounds that can invalidate a treaty, rendering it void
 ab initio. A treaty is void if it conflicts with a peremptory norm of general international law (jus
 cogens), such as a treaty authorizing genocide (Article 53). Consent to be bound may also be
 invalidated by error (Article 48), fraud (Article 49), corruption of a state representative (Article
 50), or coercion of a representative or of a state by the threat or use of force (Articles 51 and 52).
 Furthermore, a state may invoke that its consent was invalid due to a manifest violation of a
 fundamental rule of its internal law regarding treaty competence (Article 46).

The cornerstone of statutory administrative law in India is the concept of delegated legislation,
wherein the legislature delegates its law-making power to the executive. The fountainhead of this
authority is the Parent Act, also known as the enabling Act. For instance, The Air (Prevention and
Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, serves as a classic illustration; while it establishes the broad
framework for pollution control, it specifically empowers the Central Government to formulate
detailed rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act. This delegation is a practical necessity,
allowing the executive to address technical and situational details that the legislature cannot
feasibly handle.

The output of this delegated power manifests in various forms, including Rules, Regulations, By-
laws, Orders, and Notifications. While these instruments have the force of law, they are created by
administrative bodies, not Parliament. To ensure this vast power is not misused, the Indian legal
framework provides robust mechanisms of control. Paramount among these is Parliamentary
control, exercised through specialized bodies like the Committee on Subordinate Legislation in
both the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. These committees scrutinize delegated legislation to ensure
it does not exceed the authority granted by the parent Act or trespass upon citizens' rights. A key
procedural tool is the inclusion of "laying" clauses in the Parent Act, which requires that the rules
made be placed before Parliament. This allows for legislative oversight, where such rules can be
modified or annulled.

Beyond parliamentary oversight, strict procedural requirements govern the lifecycle of these rules.
The General Clauses Act, 1897, particularly Sections 20 to 22, provides the statutory backbone for
these procedures. These sections deal with the crucial aspects of when a rule is considered to have
been made and the power to bring it into force. Finally, the principle of publication is fundamental.
For any rule, regulation, or notification to acquire the binding force of law, it must be published in
the Official Gazette. This mandatory publication serves as formal notice to the public, transforming
a draft into an enforceable legal instrument and upholding the rule of law by ensuring transparency
and accessibility.

 The Stockholm Declaration, formally known as the Declaration of the United Nations Conference
 on the Human Environment, was adopted in 1972 and is widely regarded as the foundational
 instrument of modern international environmental law. Emerging from the first major global
 conference to make the environment a principal subject of international concern, the Declaration
 consisted of a preamble and twenty-six principles intended to guide the preservation and
 enhancement of the human environment. Its historical significance lies in its articulation of core
 legal concepts that would later crystallize into binding treaty obligations and customary
 international law.

 Principle 21, perhaps the most influential provision, proclaimed that states have the sovereign right
 to exploit their own resources pursuant to their own environmental policies, but also the
 responsibility to ensure that activities within their jurisdiction or control do not cause damage to
 the environment of other states or of areas beyond the limits of national jurisdiction. This carefully
 balanced formulation reconciled the competing claims of territorial sovereignty and transboundary
 environmental protection, embedding the essence of the no-harm rule into the international legal
 consciousness. The Declaration also introduced the concept that environmental protection is not
 merely a national concern but a shared responsibility of humanity, with Principle 1 declaring that
 man bears a solemn responsibility to protect and improve the environment for present and future
 generations, thereby planting the seeds of the principle of intergenerational equity.

 Furthermore, it called for international cooperation to address environmental challenges,
 encouraged the exchange of scientific information, and urged states to develop national
 environmental laws and institutions. While the Stockholm Declaration itself was not a legally

 judicial decisions, and state practice, effectively shaping the normative framework within which
 contemporary environmental governance operates. It paved the way for later developments such

 The Specific Relief Act, 1963, provides the juridical foundation for enforcing individual civil
 rights when monetary compensation is inadequate. A primary remedy under this legislation is the
 Recovering of Possession of Property, which focuses on restoring physical control over a thing
 rather than its pecuniary value. Regarding immovable property, such as land or buildings, the Act
 provides recourse for two categories of plaintiffs. First, a person who has been wrongly
 dispossessed can file a suit for possession based on their legal title, seeking to reclaim what is
 rightfully theirs. Second, and critically, the Act protects a person who may not have perfect title
 but was in prior possession. Rooted in the principle that no one should take the law into their own
 hands, it mandates that even a person with prior possession cannot be forcibly evicted; the rightful
 owner must seek recourse through due process of law. For movable property, the remedy allows a
 person entitled to immediate possession of a specific, identifiable chattel—such as a family
 heirloom, a unique piece of art, or a specific antique—to sue for the return of that exact object,
 recognizing its special value that cannot be replicated by a damages claim.

 Equally central to the Act is the remedy of Specific Performance of Contracts, which compels a
 defaulting party to actually perform the positive obligations they undertook in an agreement, rather
 than simply paying compensation for its breach. The jurisdiction of the court to grant this relief is
 guided by the Act's provisions. Specific performance is typically decreed for contracts where
 damages would be an inadequate remedy. These include contracts for the transfer of immovable
 property, like a sale of a house, where every piece of land is considered unique. It also applies to
 contracts for the transfer of movable property that has special or unique value, such as rare shares
 or heirlooms, as well as contracts involving a fiduciary relationship, where the element of personal
 trust is paramount. Conversely, the Act explicitly bars the enforcement of certain categories of
 contracts. The court will not order specific performance of contracts that require constant
 supervision, such as detailed building contracts. It also refuses to enforce contracts for personal
 service, grounded in the principle that forcing a singer to perform would amount to involuntary
 servitude. Furthermore, contracts that are vague, uncertain in their terms, or which have become
 impossible to perform will not be specifically enforced, ensuring that the court's equitable power
 is exercised only where a clear, binding obligation exists.

 Most people are aware that they procrastinate, yet awareness alone rarely cures the habit. The
 standard explanation is laziness, but psychologists have largely abandoned this account.
 Procrastination is better understood as a failure of self-regulation driven by present bias: the human

CLAT 2027 Mock Test – 18                                              12 Minutes to CLAT

 tendency to assign disproportionate weight to immediate discomfort relative to future benefit.
 When a task is unpleasant, boring, or anxiety-inducing, the emotional cost of starting it feels
 concrete and immediate, while the reward of completing it feels abstract and distant. The rational
 calculus points clearly toward starting, but the emotional calculus overrides it. This framing
 matters because it shifts the target of intervention. If procrastination were simply laziness, the
 remedy would be willpower or moral exhortation. But if it is a predictable feature of how human
 minds discount the future, more structural solutions become relevant. Breaking a task into smaller
 sub-tasks reduces the emotional cost of beginning, since each sub-task feels less overwhelming
 than the whole. Implementation intentions -- specific plans linking a situation to an action ("When
 I sit down after dinner, I will write for twenty minutes") -- exploit the brain's tendency to automate
 routine-associated behaviour, reducing the moment-to-moment decision load. Critics of the
 present-bias account argue that some procrastination is rational. Waiting for more information
 before beginning a task, or allowing unconscious processing to generate better solutions, can lead
 to higher-quality outcomes. The surgeon who delays a non-emergency procedure while reviewing
 new evidence is not behaving irrationally. Distinguishing productive delay from self-defeating
 avoidance requires attention to whether the delay is goal-directed or whether it is accompanied by
 guilt, rising anxiety, and last-minute rushes that erode the quality of the final output. The evidence
 suggests that the most effective interventions target the emotional barrier rather than the cognitive
 one. Self-compassion -- treating oneself with understanding after procrastinating rather than with
 harsh self-criticism -- consistently reduces future procrastination, possibly because guilt itself
